what_the_engine_does_today.method: flip one byte in Player-Data/7-MSpT2-128/Triples-MSpT2-P<n>, run with -F, restore. Four runs, four parties.
what_the_engine_does_today.conclusion: The transcript carries no party information at all, and the attribution a reader would reach for is actively misleading.

what_is_available_instead.why: Shamir shares of a degree-d secret are an RS[n, d+1] codeword. At n=7 and degree 2 that is RS[7,3], distance 5, so Berlekamp-Welch corrects floor(4/2) = 2 errors --- exactly T --- and the recovered polynomial names every share that does not lie on it.

what_it_costs.traffic: MP-SPDZ opens from 2t+1 = 5 of seven shares. RS[5,3] has distance 3 and locates one error, not two. Naming T = 2 needs all n, which is 40 percent more per opening.
what_it_costs.compute: tens to a few hundred microseconds per opening, in CPython
what_it_costs.rounds: none. The decode is local on data already received.

the_limits: PRODUCTS ARE WEAKER. A product before degree reduction is degree 2t, RS[7,5], distance 3, so one liar is nameable and two are not. Measured: 300/300 at one, 0/300 at two.

THREE LIARS ARE UNRESOLVABLE and the decoder says so rather than guessing. 0/300 recovered at three wrong shares, and no name is produced. That is the correct behaviour: a decoder that named somebody at three would be worse than one that gave up.

AND IT CANNOT SEE A SUBSTITUTED INPUT. This is the half that matters. secret_input() sums one additive share per party, so a party that feeds a different number is offering a valid sharing of a different value. Nothing is inconsistent and there is nothing to decode. Locating that costs n openings and n masks instead of one --- the masks being what forced the 164-bit field.
